chapters.heading: UNITED STATES CAPITOL POLICE REFORM AND ACCOUNTABILITY

sections.heading: Directives of the Board and Sergeants at Arms
paragraphs: (a) The Capitol Police Board may issue a written directive to the Chief requiring the Capitol Police to take action necessary to protect Congress, preserve order, correct neglect of duty, respond to inactivity, address a security failure, enforce this Act, maintain adequate coverage, or ensure the continued operation of either House.

(b) A directive of the Board may require the Chief to assign officers, provide security coverage, conduct patrols, secure a proceeding, respond to a threat, prepare a report, review misconduct, correct a failure in staffing, open or close an access point, provide protective services, coordinate with a Sergeant at Arms, or take another action within the lawful duties of the Capitol Police.

(c) The Chief shall carry out a lawful directive of the Board. Except where the Board expressly determines that immediate control is necessary because of neglect, refusal, emergency, inactivity, failure of command, or substantial risk to Congress, the Chief shall retain operational control over the manner in which the directive is executed.

(d) A directive of the Board shall not be used to micromanage ordinary patrol assignments, routine officer supervision, individual tactical decisions, or internal administrative matters that are properly within the day-to-day command of the Chief, unless the Board determines that such matter reflects neglect, dysfunction, failure to provide coverage, abuse of authority, or a risk to the orderly operation of Congress.

(e) The Board may require the Chief to submit an operational readiness plan, staffing plan, patrol plan, chamber security plan, access control plan, protective services plan, emergency response plan, or corrective action plan where the Board determines that the Capitol Police is not adequately performing its duties under this Act.

(f) Where the Board determines that the Capitol Police has failed to maintain adequate operations, the Board may require minimum staffing levels, minimum patrol coverage, response-time expectations, post assignments, reporting requirements, training deadlines, recruitment measures, or other corrective measures necessary to restore the functioning of the Capitol Police.

(g) The House Sergeant at Arms may issue a lawful security direction to the Chief or to officers of the Capitol Police concerning the protection of House-controlled areas, House proceedings, Members of the House, officers of the House, House employees, House witnesses, invited guests of the House, access to House spaces, or preservation of order in areas under House control.

(h) The Senate Sergeant at Arms may issue a lawful security direction to the Chief or to officers of the Capitol Police concerning the protection of Senate-controlled areas, Senate proceedings, Senators, officers of the Senate, Senate employees, Senate witnesses, invited guests of the Senate, access to Senate spaces, or preservation of order in areas under Senate control.

(i) The Sergeant at Arms of the Senate, and any deputy, assistant, officer, employee, or agent acting under the authority of the Sergeant at Arms, may enter, inspect, secure, and remain present within any Senate-controlled or Senate-related area when reasonably necessary to carry out official duties relating to security, order, access control, emergency response, protection of Senators, protection of Senate officers and employees, enforcement of Senate rules, or preservation of Senate operations.

(j) For purposes of this subsection, “Senate-controlled or Senate-related area” includes the Senate Chamber, Senate galleries, Senate cloakrooms, Senate committee rooms and hearing rooms, Senate leadership offices, Senate office buildings, Senate corridors, lobbies, entrances, stairwells, restricted access points, rooms or facilities used for official Senate proceedings, meetings, hearings, briefings, ceremonies, or security operations, and any other area placed under Senate control, Senate use, or Senate security responsibility.

(k) No Senator, officer, employee, visitor, agency representative, law enforcement officer, or other person may knowingly obstruct, deny, delay, or interfere with lawful access by the Sergeant at Arms or authorized Sergeant at Arms personnel acting under this subsection.

(l) A security direction issued by a Sergeant at Arms shall control within the controlled spaces and proceedings of that House, except where immediate compliance would create a serious risk to life, officer safety, emergency response, the security of another congressional proceeding, or the lawful operations of the Capitol Police. (m)If the Chief declines, delays, modifies, or cannot comply with a security direction issued by a Sergeant at Arms, the Chief shall state the reason for doing so and notify the relevant Sergeant at Arms and the Board as soon as practicable.

(n) Where the Chief fails or refuses to provide necessary security coverage, respond to a lawful security direction, maintain basic operations, or protect the proceedings of either House, the relevant Sergeant at Arms may temporarily direct available Capitol Police officers assigned to that House’s controlled areas.
(o) A temporary direction issued by a Sergeant at Arms shall be limited to the affected House, affected proceeding, affected controlled space, or immediate security need.

(p) A temporary direction issued by a Sergeant at Arms shall remain in effect only until the Chief resumes lawful command, the Board acts, the security need ends, or the relevant Sergeant at Arms withdraws the direction.

(q) A Sergeant at Arms exercising temporary direction under this section may direct officers to secure doors, control access, protect Members and officers, escort witnesses or guests, preserve order, respond to disruptions, remove disorderly persons, enforce chamber security rules, or take other action necessary to protect the affected House.

(r) A Sergeant at Arms exercising temporary direction under this section may not permanently reassign officers, permanently alter the command structure of the Capitol Police, issue department-wide regulations, enter into interagency agreements, impose final discipline on Capitol Police officers, or exercise authority unrelated to the affected House’s security need.

(s) The Chief shall ensure that officers assigned to House-controlled areas and Senate-controlled areas understand that lawful security directions from the relevant Sergeant at Arms are binding within those areas, subject to this Act and emergency safety limitations.
(t) The Board may review any refusal, delay, modification, or failure to comply with a directive or security direction issued under this section.

(u) Repeated failure by the Chief to carry out lawful directives of the Board, lawful security directions of a Sergeant at Arms, or basic operational duties of the Capitol Police may constitute neglect of duty, failure of command, or good cause for removal.

(v) Nothing in this section shall transfer day-to-day command of the Capitol Police from the Chief to the Board or to either Sergeant at Arms. The purpose of this section is to ensure that the Board and the Sergeants at Arms may require action when congressional security, chamber operations, or the basic functioning of the Capitol Police requires it. (w)Nothing in this subsection shall be construed to diminish the authority of the United States Capitol Police, limit the authority of the Senate or the Committee on Rules and Administration, authorize access for a personal or political purpose, authorize unnecessary disruption of official Senate proceedings, or permit the unlawful disclosure of privileged, classified, confidential, or otherwise protected information.
